content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler multiple fruit, Stage 3 is a baby food product containing a blend of several fruits, designed for the third stage of complementary feeding. The product undergoes strict quality control, contains no artificial additives, and is suitable for infants from 6 months old.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend includes apple, pear, banana and peach, providing a variety of flavors and nutrients.
All fruits are gently heat‑treated at low temperatures to preserve maximum vitamins.
The product is free from gluten, lactose and added sugar, making it safe for sensitive babies.
Packaging is made from recyclable material and meets environmental standards.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Fruit antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports growth
items.content: B‑vitamins and minerals contribute to normal nervous system development and child growth.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Some infants may have an allergic reaction to individual fruits in the blend.

items.title: Not for infants under 6 months
items.content: The product is intended for babies who have already started complementary feeding.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the container refrigerated and use within 48 hours.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The meal is ready to serve straight from the pack. If needed, thin with a small amount of breast milk or formula to achieve the desired consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 48 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Sunflower meal bread is a whole‑grain loaf that incorporates milled sunflower meal (2554) into the dough. Sunflower meal is a by‑product of oil extraction from sunflower seeds and is rich in dietary fiber, B‑vitamins, vitamin E, magnesium and phosphorus. The bread has a dense crumb, a subtle nutty aroma and a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sunflower meal is obtained after pressing oil from sunflower seeds.
It contains over 10 % dietary fiber, making it an excellent source of roughage.
Adding meal to bread boosts its nutritional value without markedly increasing calories.
Sunflower meal is high in phytosterols, which may help lower cholesterol levels.
Bread with meal is often used in diet plans and programs that promote healthy digestion.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports regular bowel movements, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E is a potent antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium is essential for muscle and nerve function and helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Phytosterols and monounsaturated fats in the meal may contribute to lower LDL‑cholesterol.

items.title: Enriched with B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Sunflower allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to sunflower or its meal.

items.title: High fiber content
items.content: Excessive fiber intake can cause bloating, gas and abdominal discomfort.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Sunflower meal contains modest amounts of oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sunflower meal bread works well for sandwiches, toast, serving alongside soups and salads. It can be toasted, crumbled into casseroles, or used as a base for breadcrumbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or cloth sack. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator in an airtight container to prevent drying out and mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Celery (Apium graveolens) is a crisp, juicy vegetable with long, ribbed stalks and leafy tops, native to the Mediterranean and southern Europe. It has a fresh, slightly salty, herbal flavor and a crunchy texture. Celery is eaten raw as a snack, in salads, and juices, and cooked in soups, stews, and stocks as a basic flavoring.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Celery is about 95 percent water.
Celery is related to parsley, carrots, and fennel, and celeriac is a root variety of the same species.
Celery seeds are used as a spice and in celery salt.
Celery, onion, and carrot form the base of many classic soups and sauces.
Both celery stalks and leaves are edible.

items.title: Hydrating and low in calories
items.content: Celery is mostly water and very low in calories.

items.title: Provides vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports normal blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains potassium and folate
items.content: These nutrients support normal blood pressure and cell function.

items.title: Contains plant compounds
items.content: Celery contains flavonoids such as apigenin and luteolin with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Celery contributes fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Celery allergy
items.content: Celery allergy can be serious, including in cooked celery and celery seed, and celery is a recognized major food allergen in many countries.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Celery contains vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Sun sensitivity
items.content: Celery contains compounds that can make skin more sensitive to sunlight in rare cases.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Wash celery thoroughly, since conventionally grown celery may carry residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Celery can be eaten raw with dips, peanut butter, or hummus, chopped into salads, or blended into juices and smoothies. It is sautéed or simmered in soups, stews, stocks, stuffing, and braises. The leaves can be used as an herb.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store celery in the refrigerator, wrapped in foil or in a container with a little water, where it usually keeps for one to two weeks. Keep cut celery in an airtight container. Celery that is limp can sometimes be revived in cold water.

content.title: About
content.content: Grape leaves are the edible leaves of the grapevine (Vitis vinifera), widely used in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Caucasian, and Central Asian cooking. They have a slightly tangy, earthy flavor and a tender texture when cooked. Fresh or brined, they are best known as the wrapper for stuffed dishes such as dolma, sarma, and tolma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffed grape leaves are known as dolma, sarma, or tolma, depending on the country.
Young, tender leaves picked in spring are the best for cooking.
Grape leaves are sold fresh, in brine in jars, or frozen.
Brined leaves should be rinsed well to remove the salty brine.
Grape leaves have been used in cooking for thousands of years in the regions where grapes are grown.

items.title: Provides vitamin K and vitamin A
items.content: Grape leaves provide vitamin K for normal blood clotting and carotenoids that the body can convert into vitamin A.

items.title: Provides vitamin C and manganese
items.content: These nutrients support the immune system and metabolism.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Grape leaves contribute fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Grape leaves contain plant compounds such as quercetin with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Grape leaves are low in calories, though stuffed dishes may be higher.

items.title: Sodium in brined leaves
items.content: Brined grape leaves can be very high in sodium, so rinse them well and check labels.

items.title: Possible medication interactions
items.content: Grape leaves contain vitamin K. People taking blood thinners should consult a healthcare professional about keeping their intake consistent.

items.title: Oxalates and tannins
items.content: Grape leaves contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit, and tannins that may reduce iron absorption.

items.title: Residues and allergies
items.content: Wash fresh leaves thoroughly, and avoid leaves from vines that may have been sprayed. Allergic reactions are possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grape leaves are rinsed, softened by blanching if fresh, and used to wrap fillings of rice, herbs, and meat, then simmered until tender. They can also be added to pickles or used to wrap fish before grilling. Serve stuffed leaves warm or cold with yogurt or lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh grape leaves in the refrigerator in a bag for several days, or blanch and freeze them. Keep unopened brined leaves in a cool, dry place and refrigerate them in their brine after opening, using them within a few weeks. Cooked stuffed leaves should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days.

content.title: About
content.content: Green olives are the unripe fruits of the olive tree (Olea europaea) harvested before they fully mature. They have a slightly bitter taste, firm flesh, and are usually fermented or brined to reduce bitterness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green olives are typically picked in late summer while still immature.
Traditional processing includes fermentation in brine, oil, or alkaline solutions to remove bitter polyphenols.
The olive tree has been a symbol of peace and victory in ancient Greece and Rome.
Olive oil derived from olives is considered one of the healthiest plant fats.
There are over 500 olive varieties, each giving a distinct flavor profile.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: Olives contain oleic acid, which supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols such as oleuropein protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in olives aids regular bowel function.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Olives provide vitamin E, iron, copper, and small amounts of calcium.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory properties
items.content: Polyphenolic compounds may help reduce inflammation in the body.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Brined olives often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Olive allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to olives or olive oil.

items.title: Olive oil sensitivity
items.content: Large amounts of olives may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Green olives are commonly served as a snack, added to salads, pasta, pizza, and tapas. They can be used in marinades, sauces, and spreads, or blended into a paste (pesto).

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep olives in their original brine in a sealed jar in the refrigerator. Properly stored, they last several months. Discard any that develop mold or an off‑odor.

pizza-cheese-with-vegetables-from-frozen.title: Cheese and Vegetable Pizza, Thin Crust (Frozen)

content.title: About
content.content: Thin frozen cheese and vegetable pizza is a convenient option for a quick lunch or dinner. The crust is thin and crispy, topped with tomato sauce, plant-based cheese, and a mix of vegetables such as bell pepper, onion, mushrooms, and olives. The pizza is designed for baking in a conventional oven or heating in a microwave.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust requires a shorter baking time than traditional thick crust.
Frozen pizzas often use pre‑cooked vegetables to preserve flavor and texture.
The cheese blend typically includes mozzarella and other melt‑friendly cheeses for even melting.
In many countries, added herbs like oregano or basil are mixed directly into the dough.
Rapid freezing technology retains most of the vitamins and minerals in the vegetables.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese provides both dairy and plant protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium, and fiber, supporting overall health.

items.title: Lower fat content with moderate consumption
items.content: Thin crust contains fewer calories than thick crust, and a moderate amount of cheese helps control saturated fat intake.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables aids regular bowel movements.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Tomatoes and vegetables are rich in lycopene and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made pizzas often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some commercial doughs may include partially hydrogenated oils that contain trans fats.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: Frozen pizzas can be calorie‑dense; it is important to follow the recommended serving size.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Preheat the oven to 200 °C (390 °F). Place the pizza on a rack or baking sheet and bake for 10–12 minutes, until the crust is golden and the cheese is fully melted. Optionally add fresh herbs before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pizza in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After thawing, cook immediately. Do not keep thawed pizza at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

stewed-seasoned-ground-beef-puerto-rican.title: Stewed seasoned ground beef, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed seasoned ground beef in Puerto Rican style is a ready‑to‑eat product made from ground beef slowly simmered with classic Puerto Rican spices: adobo, oregano, garlic, onion and a splash of vinegar. The result is a fragrant, mildly spicy dish with a deep flavor that can be used as a base for rice, beans, tacos or served on its own.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puerto Rican cuisine blends Spanish, African and Taíno culinary traditions.
Slow simmering makes the meat exceptionally tender and allows the spices to fully develop.
The traditional adobo sauce used in the recipe contains vinegar, soy sauce and dried oregano.
The dish is often served with rice and beans (arroz con gandules) – a classic Puerto Rican pairing.
Prepared beef can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or frozen for up to 3 months.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Ground beef provides a high‑quality protein source essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The iron in beef helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels and energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef is rich in B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The dish fits well into low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugars.

items.title: Benefits of spices
items.content: Oregano and garlic have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and adobo paste can raise the salt level; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow pathogenic bacteria such as Salmonella to grow.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Ground beef contains saturated fat; those monitoring cholesterol should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat the stewed beef in the microwave or on a skillet and serve with rice, beans, mashed potatoes, or use as a filling for tacos, burritos and wraps. It also works well added to soups and casseroles to boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before eating, heat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C.
